items.title: EasyBI
items.text:
A self-service BI library for WPF. The developer declares what can be analyzed, end users build their visuals by drag-and-drop, and rendering is delegated to interchangeable connectors (LiveCharts2, OxyPlot, ...).

 Source (IQueryable) ─▶ Semantic model ─▶ AnalyticQuery ─▶ ResultSet ─▶ ChartData ─▶ IVisualRenderer
                         (developer)       (end user)       (engine)     (pivot)      (connector)

  • Getting started

    Install the packages, declare a model and show your first designer.

  • Guide

    The designer, calculated measures, filters and cross-filtering.

  • Visuals

    Matrix, combined charts, conditional formatting, tooltips, legends...

  • Dashboard

    Arrange visuals, let end users build them by dragging fields.

  • Customization

    Themes, slots, localization and your own chart connector.

  • Changelog

    What changed in each version, and the breaking changes.

items.title: Projects
items.text: Project Role Dependencies EasyBI.Abstractions The contract: model, query, ResultSet, VisualDefinition, ReportDefinition none EasyBI.Core Model builder, query engine over IQueryable (expression trees), pivot, filtering, JSON Abstractions EasyBI.Wpf IVisualRenderer, EasyBIContext, VisualView, ReportDesigner, FilterBar, dashboard (DashboardPanel, DashboardView, behaviors), built-in KPI, Table, Matrix, Gauge, Text and Image renderers Core + Microsoft.Xaml.Behaviors.Wpf EasyBI.Renderers.LiveCharts2 LiveCharts2 connector (bars, stacked bars, lines, areas, points, combined charts, pies, donuts, waterfalls) Wpf + LiveCharts2 EasyBI.Renderers.OxyPlot OxyPlot connector (the same chart types) Wpf + OxyPlot EasyBI.Themes.MaterialDesign EasyBI follows a Material Design in XAML theme Wpf + MaterialDesignThemes EasyBI.Themes.WpfUi EasyBI follows a WPF UI (lepoco) theme Wpf + WPF-UI

items.title: Versions
items.text: This site documents every published version: pick one in the selector at the top of the page. dev is the development branch, not yet released. The versions published before this site show the README of their time.

items.title: Changelog
items.text: Every version, with its breaking changes. EasyBI follows Semantic Versioning: while in 0.x, breaking changes bump the minor version. The report format (easybi/v1) stays backward compatible: a newer version opens older reports, and a report using a newer feature cannot be opened by an older version.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• Cross-filtering: several selections with Ctrl+click, highlighted in their visual (#41).
  • Numeric filters: number dimensions and the measures of a visual compared with numbers (≥, <, between...) (#42).
  • Matrix crossing rows with columns, with totals at every level (#43).
  • Conditional formatting: rules, color scales, data bars and icons on the values of a measure (#44); chart points colored by them, and the zones of rules shaded (#45).
  • Donut, gauge and waterfall visual types (#46).
  • Tooltips customized by the end user (extra measures, template) and the developer (EasyBIContext.TooltipOpening) (#47).
  • Legends: position chosen per visual, long legends paged (#48).
  • Several axis fields shown as groups, and dimension values relabeled per visual (#50).
  • Formulas with dimensions: SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, COUNT, DISTINCTCOUNT and IF, with conditions (SUM([Revenue]; [Region] = "North")) (#53).
  • Measures declared in code editable in the application: QueryableSemanticModel.Formula(...), and any model measure redefined in a report, with Restore (#54).
  • Redesigned calculated measure editor: colored formula, located problems, smart suggestions, catalog in tabs, operator keypad (#55).
  • Measures used in other formulas: a calculated measure can use the report's other measures; loops are refused (#56).
  • This documentation site, with a version per release.

items.title: Fixed
items.text:
• LiveCharts2: the labels under groups turn like other category labels instead of being skipped (#51).
  • Designer: the measure preview no longer cancels a query on every keystroke (#52).

items.title: Breaking changes
items.text:
• FilterContext.Selection became Selections (one per visual), with SelectionOf, ClearSelection(visualId) and DescribeSelections; CrossFilter holds Elements (SelectedElement), its Values and filter-based constructor are gone and Filters is computed (#41).
  • ChartLegend moved from EasyBI.Core to EasyBI.Abstractions and gained Auto, Top and Left; ChartFitting.BottomLegendHeight was removed (#48).
  • ModelField.IsEditable is true for every measure (the model's ones can be redefined); use IsReportMeasure for the report's own measures. MeasureContext.Set matches a measure by model and name (#54).
  • A formula using a measure that the report redefines now reads the report's version, the model's Formula measures included (#56).
  • FieldDescriptor gained an optional Formula positional parameter: source compatible, recompile (#54).

items.title: Report format
items.text: easybi/v1, backward compatible: AnyOf filters with alternatives; comparison operators (GreaterThan, Range...); the Matrix, Donut, Gauge and Waterfall marks with an optional gauge; format on a measure; showOnChart on a rule; tooltip, legendPosition and labels on a visual. A redefinition is a measures entry named like the model's measure. Formulas may use functions and other measures.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• Modernized designer: a properties panel on the right for the selected field, filter or visual (extensible through DesignerViewModel.PropertiesBuilding), chips summed up by badges, a visual type gallery, wells that follow the visual type, undo / redo and keyboard shortcuts for the chips.
  • Customizable components: slots to add, replace or hide parts of the designer, filter bar, field list, filter editor and dashboard; the five components are lookless controls with replaceable templates.
  • Renderer options: renderers declare their own options, edited in the designer and saved with the visual; LiveCharts2 charts can scroll.
  • Designer: sort and Top N, search in the field list and in a filter's values, a message explaining why a field is refused.
  • Dashboard: item selection with the mouse and the keyboard, copy and paste with the layout (also between dashboards), moving and extending items with the keyboard, fewer columns on a narrow dashboard, only the visuals in or near view are queried.

items.title: Breaking changes
items.text:
• ReportDesigner, FieldList, FilterBar, FilterEditor and DashboardView derive from Control instead of UserControl: code relying on their former named elements uses the new properties (ReportDesigner.ViewModel, FieldList.Dimensions...) and routed commands (FilterBar.AddFilterCommand...).
  • ReportDesigner has a new default template: the ReportDesignerSlots.Sort and RendererOptions slots are replaced by Properties; chip settings moved to the properties panel.
  • DesignerViewModel.CanDrop refuses fields on a well the visual type does not use.

items.title: Report format
items.text: easybi/v1 is unchanged: renderer settings live in the existing extensions of a visual. v0.3 files load as they are.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• Calculated measures: Ratio(...) / Calculated(g => ...) for developers, and formulas end users write from the field list ([Margin] / [Revenue]), saved with the report.
  • Period filters: between two dates, or relative to today (this month, last 12 months, last year), in the designer and the filter bar.
  • Comparisons over time: previous year, change, % change, year to date per measure; KPI trends (▲ / ▼).
  • Data refresh and performance: EasyBIContext.RefreshData(model); leaner SQL GROUP BY (1.3× to 1.7× faster on SQLite with 5 million rows).

items.title: Breaking changes
items.text:
• VisualPipeline.PrepareAsync has a new optional measures parameter before the cancellation token: pass the token by name (cancellationToken: token).
  • FieldDescriptor, AnalyticQuery and ModelField gained optional positional parameters: source compatible, recompile code built against v0.2.

items.title: Report format
items.text: easybi/v1 stays backward compatible: new optional measures (report) and time (measure) properties, new filter operators Between, Current, Last, Previous. Files using them cannot be opened by v0.2.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• Dashboard built from a panel, a layout API and behaviors (#10), laid out with greedy items and no gaps (#14); visuals built by dragging fields onto it (#15).
  • Combined charts: a chart type per measure, with a secondary value axis (#11).
  • Drag and drop infrastructure, reusable by applications (#13).
  • Themes: EasyBI light and dark, following WPF UI and Material Design (#17).

items.title: Fixed
items.text: • Small LiveCharts2 and OxyPlot charts stay readable (#12).

items.title: Breaking changes
items.text: • Dashboards are laid out with greedy items in rows and columns instead of a grid with gaps (#14).

items.title: 0.1.0-beta.1 — 2026-10-16
items.text:
First published version.

  • Semantic models over IQueryable, query engine pushing filters, grouping, aggregates, sort and top to the provider.
  • Designer, visuals, LiveCharts2 and OxyPlot connectors.
  • Global filters and cross-filtering (#2).
  • English and French, with runtime language switching (#4).
  • NuGet packages published with Trusted Publishing (#3, #5).

items.title: Contributing
items.text: See AGENTS.md for the code style, language rules and Git workflow.

items.title: Building and testing
items.text:
dotnet build
dotnet test
dotnet run --project samples/EasyBI.Sample

items.title: Writing this documentation
items.text:
This site is built from the Markdown files of the docs folder with Zensical, and published on GitHub Pages:

  • Every page has an edit button that opens its Markdown file on GitHub. A change merged into develop updates the dev version of the site within minutes; nothing has to be uploaded by hand.
  • Each release tag (vX.Y.Z) publishes its own version, which becomes latest; older versions stay available in the version selector.
  • A change to the public API or to the report format updates the page that documents it, and adds an entry to the changelog under Unreleased (with Breaking changes when there are).

To preview the site locally:

pip install zensical
zensical serve

items.title: Installation
items.text:
dotnet add package EasyBI.Wpf
dotnet add package EasyBI.Renderers.LiveCharts2   # and/or EasyBI.Renderers.OxyPlot
dotnet add package EasyBI.Themes.WpfUi            # optional: if the application uses WPF UI or Material Design

EasyBI.Wpf brings EasyBI.Core and EasyBI.Abstractions. Every public WPF type is available under a single XAML namespace:

xmlns:bi="https://github.com/TheoCvg/EasyBI"

items.title: Declaring a model
items.text:
The developer declares what can be analyzed: the dimensions (analysis axes) and the measures (aggregated values) of an IQueryable, then registers the model and one or more renderers in an EasyBIContext.

var model = SemanticModel.For(dbContext.Sales, "sales", "Sales")
    .Dimension(s => s.Date, "Date")
    .Dimension(s => s.Region, "Region")
    .Dimension(s => s.Product.Category, "Category")
    .Measure(s => s.Amount, "Revenue", format: "#,##0 €")
    .Count("Number of sales");

Context = EasyBIContext.Create()
    .AddModel(model)
    .UseRenderer(new LiveCharts2Renderer())
    .UseRenderer(new OxyPlotRenderer());

With EF Core, prefer a context factory: each query opens its own DbContext, and the visuals of a dashboard run in parallel. On a shared IQueryable (other than LINQ to objects), queries run one after another, because a DbContext does not support concurrent operations.

var model = SemanticModel.For(() => dbFactory.CreateDbContext(), db => db.Sales, "sales", "Sales")
    .Dimension(s => s.Region, "Region") /* ... */;

Each visual becomes one database query (filters, grouping, aggregates, sort and top in SQL): only the aggregated rows reach the application, whatever the number of rows in the table.

items.title: Showing the designer and a visual
items.text:
<bi:ReportDesigner Context="{Binding Context}" />                             <!-- design -->
<bi:VisualView Context="{Binding Context}" Definition="{Binding Visual}" />   <!-- display -->

The designer lets end users build a visual by dragging fields; a VisualView shows a saved visual. To let them arrange several visuals, use a dashboard.

items.title: Refreshing the data
items.text:
Visuals cache their last result and query again only when their query changes. When the data behind a model changes (new rows, another source), tell them, from any thread:

Context.RefreshData("sales");   // the visuals of this model; RefreshData() for all of them

items.title: Running the sample
items.text:
dotnet run --project samples/EasyBI.Sample

The demo starts in your system language (English or French) and has a language picker in its toolbar. Its data picker switches the same sales between memory (20,000 rows) and a SQLite database of 1 or 5 million rows, generated once in %LOCALAPPDATA%\EasyBI.Sample; the toolbar shows how long the last refresh took.

items.title: Writing a connector
items.text:
A connector implements a single interface. It receives already queried and pivoted data (request.Chart: categories + series) and the raw ResultSet if needed:

public sealed class MyRenderer : IVisualRenderer
{
    public string Name => "MyLib";
    public RendererCapabilities Capabilities { get; } = new(new HashSet<MarkType> { MarkType.Bar });
    public FrameworkElement Render(RenderRequest request) { /* request.Chart.Categories, request.Chart.Series */ }
}

Each ChartSeries comes with its resolved Mark and SecondaryAxis: a connector draws every series with its own type, so one chart can mix bars, lines, areas and points.

Colors come from request.Theme: series take ColorAt(index), text Foreground, axis labels MutedForeground, grid lines GridLine, tooltips Background (each one null when the theme does not set it: keep the library's default). Draw on a transparent background, so that the chart sits on the theme's surface.

Tooltips are EasyBI's: a connector replaces its library's tooltip (or tracker) with a ChartTooltipHost (EasyBI.Wpf), and shows in it, while the pointer moves over the chart, the content of the hovered category and series:

var tooltip = new ChartTooltipHost(view);
view.MouseMove += (_, e) => tooltip.Show(HitTest(e.GetPosition(view)) is { } hit
    ? request.TooltipFor(hit.Category, [hit.Series])   // EasyBI.Core: the visual's settings and the application's changes
    : null);                                           // null hides it

Legends follow ChartFitting (EasyBI.Core), which gives the place of the legend and its pages for the chart's size, the visual's choice (request.Visual.LegendPosition) and the size of the library's entries (LegendMetrics). The host turns the pages through request.LegendPager: a connector shows the entries of its page and fits again when it changes.

void Fit()
{
    var fit = ChartFitting.Cartesian(request.Chart, view.ActualWidth, view.ActualHeight, request.Visual.LegendPosition, MyMetrics);
    var shown = ChartFitting.LegendEntries(fit, request.LegendPager);   // also tells the pager where the legend is
    for (var i = 0; i < series.Count; i++) series[i].ShowInLegend = shown(i);
}
view.SizeChanged += (_, _) => Fit();
if (request.LegendPager is { } pager) pager.Changed += (_, _) => Fit();

EasyBIContext.ResolveRenderer negotiates capabilities: the active renderer if it supports every type the visual uses (the visual's and its measures'), otherwise another plugged-in renderer, otherwise a built-in one. The designer disables the types that no renderer can draw.

items.title: Renderer options
items.text:
A connector offers settings of its own to the end user by declaring them in its capabilities: the designer shows them in the "Options" section of its properties panel (DesignerPropertySections.Options) for the visuals they apply to, as a check box, a list or a number box, and saves their values with the visual.

public RendererCapabilities Capabilities { get; } = new(marks)
{
    Options =
    [
        RendererOption.Toggle("scrollable", () => Strings.Scrollable, appliesTo: v => v.Mark.IsCartesian()),
        RendererOption.Choice("curve", () => Strings.Curve, [new("straight", () => Strings.Straight), new("smooth", () => Strings.Smooth)]),
        RendererOption.Number("barWidth", () => Strings.BarWidth, 48, minimum: 4, maximum: 120),
    ],
};

public FrameworkElement Render(RenderRequest request)
{
    var scrollable = request.Visual.GetRendererOption<bool>(Name, "scrollable");   // EasyBI.Core
    ...
}
  • Labels are functions, read when shown, so that they follow the EasyBI language (EasyBILocalization.UICulture).
  • Values are stored in VisualDefinition.Extensions, one JSON object per renderer under its name ("LiveCharts2": "{\"scrollable\":true}"); a value equal to the option's default is not stored. The settings of a renderer are kept while another one draws the visual. WithRendererOption sets one in code.
  • The LiveCharts2 connector offers Scroll bar (LiveCharts2Renderer.ScrollableOption) on cartesian charts: the chart shows the first 20 categories (ScrollWindow) above a small chart of all of them, where a band marks the visible ones; dragging on it scrolls, the mouse wheel on the chart zooms.

items.title: Localization
items.text:
EasyBI's own texts (designer, filter bar, messages, granularity and aggregation names, blank and boolean values) ship in English and French. The language can change at runtime: designer, filter bar and visuals update immediately.

EasyBILocalization.Culture = CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("fr-FR"); // null = follow CurrentUICulture

The same culture formats numbers and dates. Your semantic model captions can follow the language too: call Localize with your own resources, and every caption becomes a resource key (a missing key falls back to the caption itself).

var model = SemanticModel.For(db.Sales, "sales", "Sales")
    .Dimension(s => s.Region, "Region")
    .Measure(s => s.Amount, "Revenue")
    .Localize(MyStrings.ResourceManager);

Your own XAML texts can follow it as well with LocalizedStrings and the Localize markup extension:

public static LocalizedStrings Texts { get; } = new(MyStrings.ResourceManager);

<Button Content="{bi:Localize Save, Source={x:Static local:App.Texts}}" />

Visual and report titles are user content: they are stored as typed and not translated.

items.title: Customizing the components: slots
items.text:
The parts of the ReportDesigner, FieldList, FilterBar, FilterEditor and DashboardView are slots: named places where an application adds its own content (before or after the default content), replaces it, or hides it.

<bi:ReportDesigner Context="{Binding Context}">
    <bi:Slots.Items>
        <!-- Under the preview -->
        <bi:Slot Name="{x:Static bi:ReportDesignerSlots.Preview}">
            <Button Content="Publish" Command="{Binding DataContext.PublishCommand, RelativeSource={RelativeSource AncestorType=Window}}" />
        </bi:Slot>
        <bi:Slot Name="{x:Static bi:ReportDesignerSlots.Title}" Mode="Before"><TextBlock Text="Title:" /></bi:Slot>
        <bi:Slot Name="{x:Static bi:ReportDesignerSlots.FiltersShelf}" Mode="Hide" />
    </bi:Slots.Items>
</bi:ReportDesigner>

Slots.Add(designer, ReportDesignerSlots.Header, exportButton);              // after the default content
Slots.Add(designer, ReportDesignerSlots.Fields, help, SlotMode.Before);      // above the field list
Slots.Add(filterBar, FilterBarSlots.AddButton, myAddButton, SlotMode.Replace);
Slots.Hide(designer, ReportDesignerSlots.FieldPanel);
  • Names: ReportDesignerSlots (FieldPanel, Fields, Header, Title, VisualTypes, Shelves, AxisShelf, LegendShelf, ValuesShelf, FiltersShelf, Preview, Properties), FieldListSlots (Model, Search, Dimensions, Measures, AddMeasureButton), FilterBarSlots (Filters, Label, Slicer, AddButton, Selection), FilterEditorSlots (Values, Period) and DashboardSlots (Body, ItemContent, EmptyItemChoices, ItemToolbar). Slots can be nested: Header contains Title and VisualTypes. The band menu of a dashboard is customized through BandMenuBehavior.MenuOpening.
  • Modes: After (default), Before, Replace, Hide. Before and after are left and right of the default content, or above and below it in a vertical slot (Fields, Shelves, Preview); several slots with the same name are shown in declaration order, and the last Replace or Hide wins.
  • Data context: the content takes the data context of the place it is shown in: the DesignerViewModel in the designer, the application's in the filter bar and the field list, the SlicerViewModel in FilterBarSlots.Slicer, the FilterItemViewModel in the filter editor (shown once per filter, so its slots take a template), the DashboardItem in the dashboard item slots (commands such as DashboardCommands.RemoveItem act on the item containing them).
  • Repeated slots: an element can only be shown once. A slot shown several times (FilterBarSlots.Slicer, once per global filter, the dashboard item slots, once per item, or slots declared for several components) takes a ContentTemplate (Slots.AddTemplate(...) in code), applied to the data context of each place.
  • Inheritance: Slots.Items is inherited, so slots declared on a window or a panel apply to every component in it; the nearest declaration replaces the others. The designer opened to edit a dashboard visual takes the slots of the dashboard.
  • Custom templates: the components are lookless controls. Their default templates (Themes/*.xaml of EasyBI.Wpf) are built from SlotHosts (<bi:SlotHost Slot="..." Orientation="Vertical"> with the default content inside), so a template of the application keeps the slots it hosts. A template works with the components' read-only properties and commands: ReportDesigner.ViewModel (the template's data context); FieldList.ModelOptions, Dimensions, Measures, CanAddMeasure and AddMeasureCommand, EditMeasureCommand, DeleteMeasureCommand, ResetMeasureCommand (with ModelField.IsEditable, IsReportMeasure and IsRedefined); FilterBar.Slicers, SelectionDescription and AddFilterCommand, RemoveFilterCommand (on the slicer of its data context), ClearSelectionCommand; DashboardView.Panel and DashboardCommands.

items.title: Theming
items.text: Every EasyBI control (designer, dashboard, filter bar, field list, KPI and table renderers, chart connectors) draws with resources looked up dynamically: an application restyles EasyBI by defining them, and switches theme at runtime by replacing the dictionary that defines them. Charts follow too, without querying their data again.

items.title: Light and dark
items.text:
<Application.Resources>
    <ResourceDictionary>
        <ResourceDictionary.MergedDictionaries>
            <bi:EasyBIThemeDictionary Mode="Dark" />
        </ResourceDictionary.MergedDictionaries>
    </ResourceDictionary>
</Application.Resources>

Without it, the light theme applies. To switch at runtime, change Mode (or swap the dictionary):

foreach (var theme in Application.Current.Resources.MergedDictionaries.OfType<EasyBIThemeDictionary>())
    theme.Mode = EasyBIThemeMode.Light;

items.title: Overriding a few colors
items.text:
Define the keys you want in your resources, after the theme dictionary; the others keep the theme's values:

<SolidColorBrush x:Key="{x:Static bi:EasyBITheme.AccentBrushKey}" Color="#7C3AED" />
<bi:ChartPalette x:Key="{x:Static bi:EasyBITheme.ChartPaletteKey}">
    <Color>#7C3AED</Color>
    <Color>#F59E0B</Color>
    <Color>#10B981</Color>
</bi:ChartPalette>
<CornerRadius x:Key="{x:Static bi:EasyBITheme.CornerRadiusKey}">4</CornerRadius>

The complete list, with their light and dark values, is in Themes/Light.xaml and Themes/Dark.xaml:

Key (EasyBITheme.…) Used for BackgroundBrushKey behind the dashboard, the designer and the visual editor SurfaceBrushKey cards (dashboard items, designer preview), popups, toolbars, chart tooltips SurfaceAltBrushKey field lists, designer shelves, empty items, alternate table rows BorderBrushKey, BorderStrongBrushKey borders and separators; empty items and free spaces ForegroundBrushKey, MutedForegroundBrushKey, DisabledForegroundBrushKey text, secondary text (headers, hints, icons, axis labels), unavailable options AccentBrushKey, AccentHoverBrushKey, AccentForegroundBrushKey selection, "+" buttons, drop indicators, and the text on them AccentSoftBrushKey, AccentSoftBorderBrushKey field chips, selection chip, drop placeholders SecondarySoftBrushKey, SecondarySoftBorderBrushKey filter chips HoverBrushKey small buttons under the pointer ErrorBrushKey error messages, bad values of conditional formats SuccessBrushKey, WarningBrushKey good and middle values of conditional formats MeasureBrushKey the Σ of measures in field lists, measures in formulas FormulaFunctionBrushKey, FormulaDimensionBrushKey, FormulaTextBrushKey, FormulaNumberBrushKey the parts of a formula in the calculated measure editor (EasyBI's values in the Material Design and WPF UI mappings) GridLineBrushKey grid lines of charts and tables ChartPaletteKey (ChartPalette) colors of chart series, in order CornerRadiusKey (CornerRadius) rounding of cards

Control-specific parts have their own style keys (DashboardOverlay.PlusButtonStyleKey, FreeSpaceStyleKey, DropPlaceholderStyleKey, DragSource.PreviewStyleKey... see Dashboard and Drag and drop), and DashboardItem has an implicit style.

items.title: Standard controls
items.text: Buttons, combo boxes, text boxes and check boxes inside EasyBI have no explicit style: they take your application's implicit styles, so a control library (WPF UI, Material Design...) styles them too. EasyBI's own light and dark themes color EasyBI's surfaces, text and charts, not the standard controls: with the dark theme and no control library, they keep the system's light look.

items.title: Following a control library
items.text:
With WPF UI or Material Design in XAML, install the matching package and merge its dictionary after the library's: EasyBI's surfaces, text, accent and charts then take the library's colors, light or dark, and follow its theme switches (ApplicationThemeManager.Apply, PaletteHelper.SetTheme). Its classes are in the bi: XAML namespace.

<!-- dotnet add package EasyBI.Themes.WpfUi -->
<ResourceDictionary.MergedDictionaries>
    <ui:ThemesDictionary Theme="Dark" />
    <ui:ControlsDictionary />
    <bi:WpfUiTheme />
</ResourceDictionary.MergedDictionaries>

<!-- dotnet add package EasyBI.Themes.MaterialDesign -->
<ResourceDictionary.MergedDictionaries>
    <md:BundledTheme BaseTheme="Dark" PrimaryColor="DeepPurple" SecondaryColor="Lime" />
    <ResourceDictionary Source="pack://application:,,,/MaterialDesignThemes.Wpf;component/Themes/MaterialDesign3.Defaults.xaml" />
    <bi:MaterialDesignTheme />
</ResourceDictionary.MergedDictionaries>

WpfUiTheme.Map and MaterialDesignTheme.Map list which library resource each EasyBI key takes. For another library or an application's own design system, derive from EasyBIThemeMapping and map the keys you need; unmapped keys keep EasyBI's light values, while the keys listed in Kept (colors the system has no equivalent for, such as Material Design's success and warning) and the chart palette follow the mapped background (EasyBI's light or dark values). If the library switches theme by swapping dictionaries without notifying, call Refresh() on the mapping afterwards.

ApplicationThemeManager.Apply sets the main window's Background itself: put an EasyBI background on the window's root panel rather than on the window (as the sample does).

public sealed class MyTheme() : EasyBIThemeMapping(new Dictionary<ComponentResourceKey, object>
{
    [EasyBITheme.BackgroundBrushKey] = "MyWindowBrush",
    [EasyBITheme.AccentBrushKey] = "MyPrimaryBrush",
});

items.title: Charts
items.text: VisualView passes the theme to renderers in RenderRequest.Theme (BiTheme): the palette, and the Foreground, MutedForeground, GridLine and Background colors (hexadecimal, null when unknown). It is built by EasyBITheme.ChartTheme(element) from the resources above. A palette or colors set on EasyBIContext.Theme take precedence over the resources.

items.title: Dashboard
items.text:
Arranging visuals is a WPF concern: the report (easybi/v1) never contains a layout. The dashboard is built in three layers, each usable on its own.

The layout (DashboardLayoutDefinition) is a stack of bands, each with a mode. Its items are greedy: without a constraint, they share the room their neighbours leave, so a dashboard never has a gap.

  • Fit bands are a grid of 12 columns that fills the width. A band is a stack of lines; a line is an item, or a container (LayoutNode.Row: side by side, LayoutNode.Column: stacked) of items and containers. Along a container, constrained children keep their size (ColumnSpan in columns, RowSpan in rows) and the others share the rest; across it, every child takes the whole room. An item with a RowSpan sets the height of its line and the items next to it stretch, so items stacked beside a tall item share its height.
  • Column tiers: on a narrow panel, Fit bands show fewer columns (DashboardPanel.ColumnTiers; by default 1 column under 600 px and 6 under 960 px, ColumnTier.Defaults). Spans are scaled to the tier, a line whose items would get less than 3 columns each is broken into several lines (one item per line in a single column), and constrained items keep their proportions while filling their line. Only the display adapts: the saved layout does not change, and a resize in a tier is saved in the layout's columns (DashboardPanel.ActiveColumns, ToLayoutSpan).
  • Wrap bands start their items at DashboardPanel.MinItemWidth (or their fixed Width in pixels), break lines when the next one does not fit, then share what is left on each line. Scroll bands do the same on one line, and scroll horizontally when the items do not fit.
  • A container whose children are all constrained leaves a free space, which the dashboard offers to fill.
new DashboardLayoutDefinition
{
    Bands =
    [
        new BandLayout
        {
            Items =
            [
                new LayoutNode { VisualId = title.Id, RowSpan = 1 },                                // a whole line
                LayoutNode.Row(
                    new LayoutNode { VisualId = map.Id, ColumnSpan = 6, RowSpan = 6 },               // left half, 2 lines high
                    LayoutNode.Column(LayoutNode.Item(sales.Id), LayoutNode.Item(margin.Id))),       // stacked beside it
            ],
        },
        new BandLayout { Mode = BandMode.Scroll, Items = [LayoutNode.Item(a.Id), new LayoutNode { VisualId = b.Id, Width = 360 }] },
    ],
};

DashboardPanel shows a layout (Layout property); children are matched to its items by the attached DashboardPanel.ItemId. The geometry itself is a pure function (BandArrangement.Arrange), and the panel exposes hit tests for interactions (EdgeAt, FlowIndexAt, FreeSpaces, and CaptureGeometry to hit-test the layout from before a drag).

DashboardLayout is the static class that changes a panel's layout while keeping it consistent: AddNextTo, MoveNextTo (ItemSide.Right, Left, Below, Above), InsertAt / MoveTo (a new line), Resize, ResizeWidth, SetAuto, Remove, InsertBand, RemoveBand, SetBandMode, plus Update for custom operations, Capture (snapshot to restore) and GetLayout / SetLayout (to save and restore). Next to an item, a side along its container joins it (the line's columns are shared when it has no room left), a side across it wraps the item and the newcomer in a new container. The rules are pure functions on records in DashboardLayoutEngine, usable without any UI.

DashboardView is the ready-made (lookless) control: DashboardItems showing visuals in a DashboardPanel, with every interaction provided by a behavior (Microsoft.Xaml.Behaviors):

Behavior Feature AddButtonsBehavior "+" on the right and bottom edges of an item, "+" between lines and between bands FreeSpaceBehavior fills free spaces with a placeholder that adds an item there FieldDropBehavior makes visuals from fields dragged from a FieldList (see below) MoveBehavior grip to drag an item: a picture follows the pointer and a placeholder shows where it lands, the others making room live; near an item's edge it goes next to it (like "+"), between two lines it becomes a line, over a free space it fills it; across bands, auto-scroll near the edges; Escape cancels ResizeBehavior corner handle: constrains the item (columns and rows in a grid band, pixels and rows elsewhere) ItemToolbarBehavior automatic size (for a resized item), edit, remove; text size, bold, alignment; image fit SelectionBehavior click selects an item (Ctrl+click adds or removes it, except on a bar, slice or row of a chart, where it extends the cross-filtering: VisualView.DataSelectedEvent), click on the background unselects, drag from the background draws a selection box; arrows go to the nearest item (Shift adds it), Escape unselects KeyboardLayoutBehavior Ctrl+arrows move the selected item, Ctrl+Shift+Down/Up put it in a new band, Alt+arrows extend the selected items over the free room next to them (through the commands below) BandMenuBehavior ⋮ menu of a band: Fit / Scroll / Wrap, insert, remove (MenuOpening to customize it) BandScrollBehavior scroll bar and Shift+wheel for scrolling bands TextEditBehavior double-click a text to edit it in place UndoRedoBehavior Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y (ApplicationCommands.Undo / Redo) 
<bi:DashboardView x:Name="Dashboard" Context="{Binding Context}" Document="{Binding Dashboard}">
    <i:Interaction.Behaviors>
        <!-- Declaring a behavior replaces its default; set UseDefaultBehaviors="False" to pick them all -->
        <bi:UndoRedoBehavior MaxHistory="100" />
    </i:Interaction.Behaviors>
</bi:DashboardView>

Hooks for applications:

  • events EditVisualRequested (replace the built-in designer dialog), ImageRequested (replace the file dialog), TextEditRequested, ItemRemoving (veto), Changed (every change, with the documents before and after), DocumentLoaded;
  • the item selection: SelectedItems, SelectionChanged, Select(items, DashboardSelectionMode.Replace/Add/Toggle), SelectAll, UnselectAll, RemoveSelected and DuplicateSelected (one change each), also reached through ApplicationCommands.Delete (Del), ApplicationCommands.SelectAll (Ctrl+A) and DashboardCommands.Duplicate (Ctrl+D); DashboardItem.IsSelected for templates (the default one draws a ring) and the DashboardOverlay.SelectionBoxStyleKey style. A read-only dashboard has no selection;
  • lazy loading: only the visuals of the items in or near the visible part of the dashboard query their data (DashboardItem.IsInViewport, bound to VisualView.IsActive by the default template); the others query once they scroll into view, a change of filters or data giving them one query then. ViewportMargin sets how far ahead items load (one viewport by default), LoadsVisibleItemsOnly = false loads them all (to print or export, for instance). VisualView.IsActive = false holds back the queries of any visual;
  • keyboard layout: MoveSelected(side, toNewBand) (DashboardCommands.MoveItem and MoveItemToNewBand, Ctrl+arrows and Ctrl+Shift+Down/Up; DashboardLayoutEngine.Step): Down takes an item sharing its line to a new line below; alone on its line, it joins the next line, and from the last line it goes into the band below (created past the last one); Up the same upwards, so that Down and Up undo each other; Ctrl+Shift+Down/Up puts it in a new band below/above; Left/Right swap it with its neighbour. ExtendSelected(width) (DashboardCommands.ExtendItem, Alt+arrows; DashboardLayoutEngine.Fill) extends the selected items over the free room next to them without shrinking their neighbours;
  • copy and paste of the selected items, possibly between dashboards: CopySelected / CutSelected / Paste (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X, Ctrl+V through ApplicationCommands; CreateCopy and Paste(data) work without the clipboard). The clipboard holds an easybi/v1 report (format VisualTransfer.ClipboardFormat) with the visuals and the calculated measures they use, plus their titles as text, and their layout (format DashboardView.LayoutClipboardFormat: their arrangement and sizes, DashboardLayoutEngine.Extract). Pasted items get new ids, keep their arrangement and sizes, and go after the line of the last selected item, or at the end (DashboardLayoutEngine.Insert; lines of a grid band join the anchor's grid band, other bands come as new bands); without the layout format, each one goes to the right of the previous one. Visuals of a model the context does not know are left out, and a calculated measure whose name is taken by another definition is renamed (VisualTransfer in EasyBI.Core);
  • DashboardCommands (AddVisual, AddText, AddImage, EditItem, RemoveItem, ResetSize, AddRight, AddBelow, InsertBand, RemoveBand, Duplicate, MoveItem, MoveItemToNewBand, ExtendItem — the last three take an ItemSide or its name, as CommandParameter="Below"...) for custom templates, and public methods (AddNextTo, AddIn a free space, InsertLine, SetAutoSize, SetVisual, InsertBand, BeginEdit to group changes into one undo step...);
  • a default template for DashboardView (its Panel in a scroll viewer, under an AdornerDecorator where behaviors draw: a custom template shows it with <ContentPresenter Content="{Binding Panel, RelativeSource={RelativeSource TemplatedParent}}" />), an implicit style for DashboardItem (lookless control) and the DashboardOverlay style keys (PlusButtonStyleKey, IconButtonStyleKey, GripStyleKey, ResizeGripStyleKey, FreeSpaceStyleKey, DropPlaceholderStyleKey, DragGhostStyleKey) to restyle;
  • DashboardBehavior as a base class for new interactions: it gives access to the view, the panel and the overlay where behaviors draw their controls; DragGesture handles press-drag-release gestures (with auto-scroll: AutoScroll, ScrollsBands).

IsReadOnly="True" hides the editing chrome; clicks keep cross-filtering in every mode.

Building visuals by dragging fields. FieldList shows the fields of the context's models (model picker, dimensions, measures) and drags them as ModelFields. Placed next to a dashboard, it lets users build it directly:

<DockPanel>
    <bi:FieldList DockPanel.Dock="Left" Width="210" Context="{Binding Context}" />
    <bi:DashboardView Context="{Binding Context}" />
</DockPanel>
  • dropped where an item can go (an edge, between two lines, a free space, a scrolling or wrapping band), a field makes a new visual: a KPI for a measure, the first measure by that dimension for a dimension (a line by month for a date, bars otherwise); the other items make room live around a placeholder;
  • dropped on an empty item, it fills it; dropped on a visual, it is added to it (a measure to its values, a dimension to its axis, then its legend; a dimension breaks a KPI down into bars);
  • the rules are pure functions in FieldVisuals (Create, AddField); FieldDropBehavior.CreateVisual and AddField replace them. Each drop is one undo step.

The designer's field panel is the same FieldList (its shelves accept the ModelFields of the selected model). A search box at the top of the field list (FieldList.Search) and above the values of a filter (from 8 values on, FilterItemViewModel.Search; checked values that are not shown stay checked) narrow the lists down: case and accents are ignored and every word must appear (TextMatch.Matches in EasyBI.Core).

In the designer, the visual is sorted from the properties of a chip of the Axis or Values well (ascending ↑ or descending ↓; one sorted field at a time, the sort following the field when its aggregation or grain changes). The visual's properties recall the active sort and limit the visual to its first rows (Top). DashboardDropTarget.Find, the place an item dropped at a point goes, is shared by moves and field drops.

items.title: Drag and drop
items.text:
The designer's drag and drop is built on reusable attached properties (namespace EasyBI.Wpf.DragAndDrop, XAML prefix bi:), usable on any ItemsControl of an application. Being attached properties, they can be set from a style:

<!-- Items can be dragged: a preview follows the pointer, a moved item is dimmed -->
<ListBox ItemsSource="{Binding Fields}" bi:DragSource.IsEnabled="True" bi:DragSource.AllowedEffects="Copy" />

<!-- Drops are decided by an IDropHandler (usually the view-model); an insertion line shows where the item goes -->
<ItemsControl ItemsSource="{Binding Columns}" bi:DropTarget.Handler="{Binding}" bi:DropTarget.Key="Columns" />

public sealed class MyViewModel : IDropHandler
{
    public DragDropEffects DragOver(DropInfo drop) => drop.Item is Field ? DragDropEffects.Copy : DragDropEffects.None;
    public void Drop(DropInfo drop) => Columns.Insert(drop.Index, ((Field)drop.Item!).ToColumn());
}
  • DropInfo gives the dragged Item, the target's Key (one handler for several targets), the insertion Index among the target's items and the raw Data for drags coming from elsewhere.
  • DropTarget.IsDragOver is true while an accepted drag is over the target (style triggers); DropTarget.Orientation switches the insertion rules to a vertical stack.
  • A handler may explain a refusal (IDropHandler.RefusalReason, optional): the reason is shown under the target and set on it as DropTarget.Refusal while the drag is over it.
  • A scrollable target, or its scroll viewer, scrolls when the pointer nears its edges (AutoScroller, also usable on its own); InsertionIndex holds the pure insertion rules.
  • Style keys DragSource.PreviewStyleKey (a ContentControl; DragSource.PreviewTemplate sets the content), DropTarget.InsertionLineStyleKey (a Border) and DropTarget.RefusalStyleKey (a ContentControl holding the reason).

In the designer, fields are dropped between chips, chips are reordered within a shelf, and dimensions move between Axis and Legend keeping their granularity. A refused field says why (DesignerViewModel.RefusalReason): only measures in Values, only dimensions elsewhere, a field already on the shelf, a full axis, a field of another model.

items.title: Calculated measures
items.text:
A measure is a row value that the end user aggregates (sum, average...). Ratios need more: the margin rate of a region is its total margin divided by its total revenue, not the average of its sales' rates. Calculated measures are computed from the rows of each group, inside the same query (in SQL with EF Core), and can be sorted and limited like the others; the end user cannot change their aggregation.

model
    .Ratio(s => s.Margin, s => s.Amount, "Margin rate", "MarginRate", format: "P1")      // Σ margin / Σ revenue
    .Ratio(s => s.Amount, s => 1, "Average basket", "AverageBasket", format: "#,##0 €")   // Σ revenue / number of sales
    .Calculated(g => g.Sum(s => s.Amount) - g.Sum(s => s.Cost), "Gross profit", "GrossProfit");

Ratio is empty when the denominator sums to zero. With Calculated, guard divisions yourself: some databases fail on a division by zero.

A measure can also be declared as a formula, written as end users write theirs (see below) with the names of the fields declared before it. It runs inside the query too, and end users can read and rewrite it:

model.Formula("SUM([Amount]; [Channel] = \"Web\") / [Amount]", "Web share", "WebShare", format: "P1");

An invalid formula, or one using a field declared after it, throws an ArgumentException. FieldDescriptor.Formula gives the formula of such a measure.

End users create their own from the field list (+ Calculated measure, then ✎ and ✕ on hover): a name, a format and a formula over the model's fields, typed with their captions and checked as it is typed, with its total as a preview. The editor colors the formula and underlines its problem, shows how to write the function the caret is in, offers the operators as a keypad (calculation, comparison, logic) and the functions, measures and dimensions in tabs to search and insert. Its suggestions only offer what can be written where the caret is: in the value of SUM(, the measures and number dimensions; in a condition, the dimensions; after [Region] =, the values of Region; after a value in a condition, AND and OR. Every item and operator has a help tooltip (a plain content, so tooltips keep the application's style). FormulaEditing (Tokenize, Calls, CallAt, CompletionAt, ContextAt) and MeasureFormula.Check (the problem and where it is written) give the same help to an application that builds its own editor, and CalculatedMeasureEditor exposes it as a view-model (Tabs, Search, OperatorGroups, Suggest, Accept, Insert, CurrentCall, Problem):

[Margin] / [Revenue]            ([Revenue] - [Margin]) / [Number of sales]            [Margin] * 100 / [Revenue]
SUM([Quantity] * [Unit price])  SUM([Revenue]; [Region] = "North") / [Revenue]        DISTINCTCOUNT([Customer])
COUNT([Channel] = "Web" AND [Date] >= "2024-01-01")                                   IF([Revenue] > 1000; [Margin]; 0)

A measure on its own is aggregated as in the field list. The aggregation functions SUM, AVERAGE (or AVG), MIN, MAX, COUNT and DISTINCTCOUNT compute a value from the rows of each group, like the measures declared in code: inside them, measures and dimensions are read row by row, and an optional last argument keeps only the rows matching a condition (COUNT() counts the rows, COUNT(condition) those matching it; DISTINCTCOUNT does not count empty values). IF(condition; value if true; value otherwise) works on the group or on each row; without its last value, it is empty. Conditions compare values with = <> < <= > >= (texts and yes/no values with = and <> only) and combine them with AND, OR and NOT; TRUE and FALSE are the yes/no values. The operators are + - * / with parentheses; numbers take a decimal point, texts and dates go in double quotes ("North", "2024-12-31"), and the arguments are separated by ; or ,. A division by zero gives an empty value. A dimension cannot be used outside a function, nor a measure calculated by the model (Ratio, Calculated) inside one. The formula runs in the same query as the other measures (in SQL with EF Core: CASE WHEN, COUNT(DISTINCT ...)). MeasureFormula.Functions lists the functions with their usage and description in the EasyBI language. These measures live in EasyBIContext.Measures (one context per open report): every field list, designer and visual of the context sees them, and a DashboardView loads and saves them with its document (undo does not remove them). An application that saves reports without a dashboard puts Context.Measures.Measures in ReportDefinition.Measures and loads them back with Context.Measures.Load(...).

A formula can use the report's other measures, like those of the model: with [Cost] = [Revenue] - [Margin], the cost rate is [Cost] / [Revenue]. They are computed for each group, so they are used on their own, not inside a function, and they are expanded into the same query (a visual's query carries the measures its measures use: MeasureContext.Needed, UsedBy). A measure cannot use itself, even through others ("A measure cannot use itself: this measure → [Cost] → this measure"), which is checked as it is typed and when a report is opened. Deleting a measure names the measures that use it (MeasureContext.Using); copied visuals take the measures they use along, and the formulas of pasted measures follow those that are renamed (MeasureFormula.Rename). MeasureFormula.Validate, Check and ToDisplay take the report's measures and the name of the measure being written.

End users can also change the measures declared in code (✎ on any measure): the editor starts from the measure's formula, or from the measure alone ([Revenue]) for one declared with Measure, Ratio or Calculated. Their version is saved in the report as a calculated measure named like the model's measure, which redefines it for the whole report (every visual showing it follows): a formula that is only the measure itself keeps the model's computation and the aggregation each visual chooses, and only changes the caption and the format; any other formula replaces the computation (AVERAGE([Revenue]) changes the aggregation), the measure's name in it still meaning the model's definition. Every other formula, the model's ones (Formula) included, reads a redefined measure as the report defines it. ↺ in the field list, or Restore in the editor, removes the redefinition. MeasureContext merges both (MeasuresOf, GetField, Definition), and pasting a visual never redefines the target's measures: a copied redefinition is added as a calculated measure of its own.

items.title: The designer
items.text:
The ReportDesigner has three zones: the fields on the left, the wells and the preview in the middle, the properties on the right (both side panels fold: IsFieldPanelOpen, IsPropertiesPanelOpen).

  • Chips show their field and badges summing their settings up (Σ, avg, Quarter, PY, Y2, ↓...). A click selects one (DesignerViewModel.SelectedItem) and the properties panel shows its settings in sections: aggregation, granularity, time calculation, chart type, secondary axis, sort for a field; the editor of a filter. Without a selection it shows the visual's: title, sort, Top N, its tooltips (charts), and the options of the renderer.
  • The visual type is chosen in a gallery grouped by use (comparison, trend, composition, indicators and tables); types no renderer draws are greyed.
  • Wells follow the type: a pie shows "Category" and "Value", a table "Rows", a KPI only "Values", only charts "Tooltip"; a well the type does not use refuses fields and stays shown while it still holds some. Empty wells say what to drop, and while a field or a chip is dragged the wells that accept it light up (DragSource.DragStarted).
  • Undo and redo every change of the visual (Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y or Ctrl+Shift+Z, the header's buttons, UndoCommand/RedoCommand; 100 steps, MaxHistory). Loading another visual starts a new history.
  • Keyboard: arrows go from chip to chip (Up/Down from well to well), Ctrl+Left/Right move the selected chip within its well, Delete removes it, Escape selects the visual again.

Everything stays replaceable: the template is lookless and made of slots (see below); the properties are descriptors (DesignerProperty: toggle, choice, number, text, info or any object shown with its DataTemplate, grouped in DesignerPropertySections), which DesignerViewModel.PropertiesBuilding lets an application add, remove or reorder; each kind of editor is a DataTemplate under a DesignerPropertyTemplates key; the icons of the types are geometries under VisualTypeIcons keys.

designer.ViewModel!.PropertiesBuilding += (_, e) =>
{
    if (e.Selection is ShelfItemViewModel { IsValue: true } chip)
        e.Sections.Add(new DesignerPropertySection("Notes", () => "Notes",
            [DesignerProperty.Text("Comment", () => "Comment", () => Comments.Get(chip), text => Comments.Set(chip, text))]));
};

items.title: Filtering: global filters and cross-filtering
items.text:
A FilterContext holds the filtering state of a dashboard. Set once on the container (it is an inherited property), it is used by the FilterBar and by every VisualView:

<DockPanel bi:VisualView.FilterContext="{Binding Filters}">
    <bi:FilterBar DockPanel.Dock="Top" Context="{Binding Context}" />
    <!-- ... the dashboard's VisualViews ... -->
</DockPanel>
  • Global filters (slicers): added from the FilterBar, they apply to every visual of the same model and are saved with the report (ReportDefinition.Filters).
  • Cross-filtering: clicking a bar, a point, a slice or a table row filters the other visuals of the same model on the element's dimensions (axis, plus legend for a bar). Ctrl+click adds an element to the selection of its visual, or removes it: the other visuals keep the rows of any selected element. Ctrl+click in another visual adds that visual's own selection (FilterContext.Selections, one per visual): a visual is filtered by the selections of all the others, "(Region = North or South) and Channel = Web". A plain click replaces every selection, clicking the only selected element again clears it. A visual is not filtered by its own selection: it dims what is left out of it and shows a summary of it, whose ✕ clears it (ClearSelection(visualId)); the FilterBar sums them all up and clears them all. Periods (quarter, month...) filter through FilterSpec.Grain.
  • Period filters: a date dimension, in the FilterBar or on the designer's Filters shelf, is filtered on a period rather than on a list of values: between two dates, the current day / month / quarter / year, the last n (current one included: "Last 12 months") or the n previous complete ones ("Last month"). Relative periods are resolved when the query runs, so a saved report keeps showing the last 12 months; the date column is compared to the period's bounds (date >= start AND date < end), so a database can use an index on it.
  • Numeric filters: a number dimension, in the FilterBar or on the designer's Filters shelf, is filtered on a list of values or compared with numbers: between two numbers (inclusive, one end may stay open), greater / less than, at least / at most. A measure dropped on the designer's Filters shelf filters the visual's groups by their aggregated value ("regions whose revenue ≥ 10,000"): the comparison runs after the grouping (SQL HAVING), before the sort and Top. Calculated measures can filter too, shown or not. Measures only filter a visual: their meaning depends on its grouping, so the FilterBar and the report's filters do not offer them.
PeriodFilters.Relative("Date", FilterOperator.Last, DateGrain.Month, 12);     // last 12 months
PeriodFilters.Between("Date", new DateOnly(2024, 1, 1), null);                // since January 1st, 2024
PeriodFilters.Describe(filter);                                               // "Last 12 months", localized
NumericFilters.Range("Quantity", 10, null);                                   // Quantity >= 10
NumericFilters.Compare("Amount", FilterOperator.GreaterThanOrEqual, 10_000);  // on a measure: groups >= 10,000
NumericFilters.Describe(filter);                                              // "≥ 10,000", localized

A connector only has to call request.Select?.Invoke(new CategorySelection(category, series)) on click (or RowSelection for a table): Select is null when interactivity is disabled, for example in the designer preview. When the visual is the source of the selection, request.Highlight lists the selected elements: draw them as usual and the others with SelectionFilters.DimmedOpacity, using request.IsEmphasized(category, series) (or IsRowEmphasized(row)). The OxyPlot connector dims bars and slices one by one, but lines and points by series only.

items.title: Known limitations
items.text:
• A filter on a measure compares the measure as the model aggregates it, whatever aggregation the visual shows.
  • Relative periods ("last 12 months") are resolved in the local time zone when a visual queries; an open dashboard does not query again at midnight.
  • Top applies to aggregated rows, not to categories when a legend is present.
  • Grouping, sorting and Top are pushed down to the provider, and execution is asynchronous when the source implements IAsyncEnumerable (EF Core). The SQL translation was checked manually with EF Core 8 on SQLite (every query shape, including date granularities, navigation properties and sort on an aggregate); there is no automated test against a database. SQLite cannot sum decimal columns (EF Core refuses the query).
  • At most 4 grouping dimensions (axis + legend).
  • The built-in light and dark themes do not restyle standard controls (buttons, combo boxes...): use a control library for those (see Following a control library).
  • EasyBI.Themes.WpfUi is checked against WPF UI's light and dark themes; its high contrast themes are not verified.
  • Dashboard images are embedded in the file (2 MB by default, DashboardView.MaxImageBytes).

items.title: Report format (easybi/v1)
items.text:
{
  "schema": "easybi/v1",
  "title": "Dashboard",
  "visuals": [
    {
      "title": "Revenue by region and channel",
      "model": "sales",
      "mark": "Bar",
      "axis": [ { "field": "Region", "grain": "None", "labels": { "Île-de-France": "IDF" } } ],
      "legend": { "field": "Channel", "grain": "None" },
      "legendPosition": "Bottom",
      "values": [ { "measure": "Amount" }, { "measure": "Count", "mark": "Line", "secondaryAxis": true } ],
      "tooltip": { "showPercent": true, "values": [ { "measure": "Quantity" } ], "template": "{category}: {value}" },
      "filters": [
        { "field": "Product.Category", "operator": "In", "values": [ "Services" ] },
        { "field": "Date", "operator": "Last", "values": [ "12" ], "grain": "Month" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "filters": [
    { "model": "sales", "filter": { "field": "Region", "operator": "In", "values": [ "North", null ] } }
  ]
}

null in values means a missing value. Besides In and NotIn, a date filter's operator can be Between (values: from and to as yyyy-MM-dd, inclusive, null for an open end), Current, Last or Previous (value: the number of periods; grain is their unit). A number dimension or, in a visual, a measure can be compared: GreaterThan, GreaterThanOrEqual, LessThan, LessThanOrEqual (value: the number, invariant) or Range (values: minimum and maximum, inclusive, null for an open end). An AnyOf filter keeps the rows matching every filter of one of its alternatives (its field and values are empty): cross-filtering builds one when several selected elements differ on more than one dimension, { "field": "", "operator": "AnyOf", "values": [], "alternatives": [[...], [...]] }. EasyBIContext.Validate(report) reports the unknown models and fields of a loaded report, and the formulas that no longer match their model.

Calculated measures created by the end user are saved with the report (the property is omitted when there are none), and visuals reference them by name like a field:

"measures": [
  { "name": "calc_3f9a1c0d2b7e", "caption": "Margin rate", "model": "sales", "formula": "[Margin] / [Amount]", "format": "P1" },
  { "name": "Amount", "caption": "Average revenue", "model": "sales", "formula": "AVERAGE([Amount])", "format": "N0" }
]

A measure named like a measure of its model (the second one) redefines it in the report; an empty caption keeps the model's.

Text and image visuals carry their content and no model:

{ "mark": "Text", "text": { "text": "Sales dashboard", "fontSize": 24, "isBold": true, "alignment": "Left" } }
{ "mark": "Image", "image": { "data": "iVBORw0KGgo...", "mediaType": "image/png", "fit": "Contain" } }

items.title: Dashboard file (easybi-dashboard/v1)
items.text:
DashboardSerializer saves what a DashboardView shows: the unchanged report next to the WPF layout, which references visuals by id. Sizes that are not saved are greedy. It also opens a plain easybi/v1 report (visuals then get a default layout).

{
  "schema": "easybi-dashboard/v1",
  "report": { "schema": "easybi/v1", "visuals": [ ... ], "filters": [ ... ] },
  "layout": {
    "columns": 12,
    "rowHeight": 110,
    "bands": [
      {
        "mode": "Fit",
        "items": [
          { "visualId": "...", "rowSpan": 1 },
          { "split": "Row", "children": [ { "visualId": "...", "columnSpan": 6 }, { "visualId": "..." } ] }
        ]
      },
      { "mode": "Scroll", "items": [ { "visualId": "...", "width": 360 }, { "visualId": "..." } ] }
    ]
  }
}

The same file renders identically with any connector.

items.title: Several axis fields
items.text:
An axis with several fields (Month, then Region) is drawn as a hierarchy: each bar labelled by the innermost field ("North"), each outer value once, centered under its group of bars ("2024-01"), with a line between the groups. When the bars are too narrow for their labels, every n-th group label shows, and the innermost labels give way to the groups' when fewer than two a group would fit. Categories not ordered by their outer fields (sorted on a measure) keep joined labels ("2024-01 / North"). Tooltips keep the whole category.

CategoryLevels.Of(request.Chart) (EasyBI.Core) gives a connector the short labels and the groups of each outer field (CategoryGroup: label, first category, count, center); LiveCharts2 draws the groups on extra X axes, OxyPlot on axes of the next tiers.

items.title: Combined charts
items.text:
The cartesian chart types (Bar, StackedBar, Line, Area, Scatter) can be mixed in one chart, one per measure: MeasureRef.Mark overrides the visual's type for that measure's series (with a legend, every series of the measure keeps its type), and MeasureRef.SecondaryAxis draws it against a second value axis on the right. In the designer, each measure of a chart has a type selector and a "Y2" toggle. These settings only change the drawing: the query is the same, so changing them does not query the source again.

new VisualDefinition
{
    Model = "sales",
    Mark = MarkType.Bar,                                      // default type of the measures
    Axis = [new("Date", DateGrain.Quarter)],
    Values =
    [
        new("Amount"),                                        // bars
        new("Margin") { Mark = MarkType.Line },               // line
        new("Count") { Mark = MarkType.Scatter, SecondaryAxis = true }, // points, right axis
    ],
};

items.title: Conditional formatting
items.text:
Each measure of a table, a matrix or a KPI can have a format (MeasureRef.Format, a ValueFormat), edited in the designer's properties panel when its chip is selected ("Formatting" section). It holds:

  • a fixed style: text color, bold, italic, alignment;
  • rules, checked in order, the first matching one applies: a comparison (GreaterThan... Range, as in numeric filters) and the text color, background and weight it gives;
  • a color scale: a background going from one color to another (optionally through a middle one) between the smallest and the largest value shown;
  • data bars: a bar in the cell as long as the value compared with the largest one (negative values in their own color);
  • icons (arrows, triangles, circles) for high, middle and low values, split at two thresholds or, without them, in thirds.

Colors are the theme's (ThemeColors: accent, success, warning, error, muted), which follow light and dark themes and control libraries, or a custom #RRGGBB. As backgrounds, the theme's colors are softened with the theme's background so that values stay readable. The scale, the bars and the automatic thresholds compare a value with the cells shown, not with the totals; a matrix leaves its totals unformatted. A format only changes the drawing: the source is not queried again. ValueStyler (Core) computes the ValueStyle of a value for any renderer, and the FormattedValue control (lookless) draws it in the built-in grids.

In charts, the rules and the color scale color each bar, point and slice (LiveCharts2's conditional draw: OnPointMeasured gives each point its paint; OxyPlot colors bars and slices one by one, not the points of lines). Stacked bars are judged as a whole and keep their legend colors: a rule or a scale compares the total of the stack, and frames the whole stack in its color (ChartFormatting.StackOutlines). The designer's editor only shows what the visual's type uses (on a chart: the rules' color and zone, and the scale; on a KPI: no scale or bars); what it hides is kept. A rule with "show its zone on charts" (FormatRule.ShowOnChart) shades its zone of the value axis: from its value up for "greater than", down for "less than", between its bounds for a range, labelled with the condition (RectangularSection in LiveCharts2, RectangleAnnotation in OxyPlot). ChartFormatting.For(request) (Core) gives a connector the color of each point (PointColor) and the zones (Bands); each ChartSeries carries the MeasureKey of its measure.

new MeasureRef("Amount")
{
    Format = new ValueFormat
    {
        Rules = [new FormatRule { Operator = FilterOperator.LessThan, Value = 1000, Color = ThemeColors.Error, IsBold = true }],
        Bar = new DataBar(),
        Icons = new IconSet { Kind = IconKind.Triangles },
    },
};

A pie (MarkType.Pie) is a full disc; a donut (MarkType.Donut) is a ring with the total of its value in its hole (ChartCenterLabel, which places a text in the middle of a connector's plot area).

A gauge (MarkType.Gauge) shows a single value on a half circle, drawn by the built-in GaugeRenderer whatever the connector. Its scale and target are numbers of the visual (VisualDefinition.Gauge, a GaugeSettings, edited in the designer's Visual section): Minimum (empty: 0), Maximum (empty: a round number above 0, the value and the target, see GaugeScale) and Target, marked on the arc. The measure's format colors the value and adds its icon.

A waterfall (MarkType.Waterfall) shows how each category's value adds to the running total, up in the theme's success color, down in its error color, and ends with a bar of the total (Waterfall.Of gives any connector the steps and the chart with its "Total" category). It takes an axis and a single value; LiveCharts2 draws it with candles, OxyPlot with interval bars. A rule of the measure's format colors the steps it matches; clicking a step cross-filters on its category.

Besides charts, KPIs, tables and matrices, a visual can be a text (MarkType.Text, content in VisualDefinition.Text) or an image (MarkType.Image, embedded as base64 in VisualDefinition.Image). They query no model and are drawn by the built-in TextRenderer and ImageRenderer.

items.title: Legends
items.text:
A chart places its legend from its size: on the right, then below, then hidden. The end user can choose another place in the designer's Visual section (Legend: automatic, right, bottom, top, left or hidden), saved in VisualDefinition.LegendPosition (ChartLegend, omitted when Auto). A chosen side applies while the chart has room for it, otherwise the automatic place does.

Legends keep their library's look. When a legend has more entries than its room shows (a column on a side, a row above or below), it shows them by pages: a small pager (◀ 2/5 ▶, ChartLegendPager, restyled like any lookless control) appears over the chart in the corner next to the legend; its buttons and the mouse wheel turn the pages. (OxyPlot names the slices of a pie around it instead of in a legend: a hidden legend drops those names.)

items.title: Matrix
items.text:
A matrix (MarkType.Matrix) crosses its axis, the rows (up to four dimensions), with its legend, the columns, for each measure in Values, and adds the total of each row, of each column and of the whole. Each total is the measure computed on all the rows it covers (an average stays an average), not a sum of cells: VisualPipeline.PrepareAsync runs one query per level (MatrixBuilder) and hands the pivoted data to the renderer in RenderRequest.Matrix (MatrixData). The sort, Top and the filters on measures choose the rows; the column totals then only count those rows. Without columns, a matrix lists its rows and their totals with a total row. Clicking a cell cross-filters on its row and column, a row header or total on the row, a column total on the column (MatrixSelection). The built-in MatrixRenderer draws it in a grid styled like the table; in the designer, the wells of a matrix are Rows, Columns and Values.

new VisualDefinition
{
    Model = "sales",
    Mark = MarkType.Matrix,
    Axis = [new("Product.Category")],                         // rows
    Legend = new("Date", DateGrain.Year),                     // columns
    Values = [new("Amount")],
};

items.title: Comparisons over time
items.text:
Each measure of a visual can be seen through time (MeasureRef.Time, the "Calculation" list of a measure chip in the designer): its value, its value the previous year, the change since (in value or in %), or its total since the start of the year along the date axis.

Values = [new("Amount"), new("Amount") { Time = TimeCalculation.PercentChangeFromPreviousYear }],
Filters = [PeriodFilters.Relative("Date", FilterOperator.Current, DateGrain.Year)],   // this year vs last year

The previous year is the same query with its dates shifted back one year (period filters, clicked periods), run once more and matched on the groups (each month with the same month a year earlier, per series). It needs a date on the axis or a date filter, and is empty otherwise. The year-to-date total adds the values up along the date axis and starts again each year. A KPI shows a change with ▲ / ▼ in the measures' or the error color. This runs in VisualPipeline.PrepareAsync (ISemanticModel.ExecuteWithTimeAsync) on top of any model.

items.title: Tooltips
items.text:
Hovering a bar, a point, a slice or a step shows an EasyBI tooltip, the same with every connector: the category, then each hovered series with its color and value. The end user sets it up per chart in the designer:

  • the Tooltip well takes measures shown in the tooltip only (they are queried with the chart, but are no series);
  • the Tooltips section of the properties shows or hides the tooltips, the category, the series' names and each value's share of its series' total (%), and takes a custom text replacing the content, with fields between braces: {category}, {series}, {value}, {percent} and any measure of the chart or of the well, by name or caption ("{category}: {value} for {Quantity} sales"; an unknown field stays as typed).

The settings are saved with the visual (VisualDefinition.Tooltip, a TooltipSettings, omitted when it has none).

For the developer, the content is a TooltipContent (a Title, Items of label, value and color, or a Text):

  • Change it for every chart, before it opens: EasyBIContext.TooltipOpening gives the visual, the hovered category and series and EasyBI's content; replace Content, or set it to null to show nothing.
context.TooltipOpening += (_, e) =>
{
    if (e.Visual.Model == "sales" && e.Content is { } content)
        e.Content = content with { Items = [.. content.Items, new TooltipItem("Target", Targets.For(content.Title))] };
};
  • Restyle it: the frame is a standard ToolTip (it takes the application's tooltip style) and the content is drawn by a DataTemplate under ChartTooltips.TemplateKey, which an application replaces in its resources:
<DataTemplate x:Key="{x:Static renderers:ChartTooltips.TemplateKey}">
    <StackPanel>
        <TextBlock Text="{Binding Title}" FontWeight="Bold" />
        <ItemsControl ItemsSource="{Binding Items}" DisplayMemberPath="Value" />
    </StackPanel>
</DataTemplate>
  • Build it without a view: Tooltips.Build(request, category, series) (EasyBI.Core) gives the default content of a RenderRequest.

items.title: Value labels
items.text: A visual can show its own text for values of a dimension: "IDF" for "Île-de-France". Selecting a dimension's chip in the designer shows Value labels: pick a value (type to search among many), type its text and add it; each label can be edited or removed. The labels apply everywhere in the visual (axis, groups, legend, tooltips, tables, matrices, the selection's description); filters and cross-filtering keep the values themselves. They are saved with the visual's field (FieldRef.Labels, keyed by the value's invariant text, omitted when there are none); field.Display(value) and field.WithLabel(value, text) (EasyBI.Core) read and set them. Dates have none: their periods follow their grain.
